title: A radio map resolves nearly 63,000 cosmic sources in one patch of sky
freshness: Preprint first released November 4, 2026, reported accepted by Astronomy & Astrophysics; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: LOFAR has produced an unusually sharp, deep radio view of a small region of sky. Combining new observations with an earlier map yields 62,916 sources, helping astronomers distinguish star formation from black-hole jets.
whyItMatters: The map makes faint radio structures easier to separate and identify, opening more precise studies of how galaxies form stars and how their central black holes affect surrounding gas.

body:
## A sharper view of the radio sky

A patch of sky that looks nearly empty to the naked eye can be crowded with radio sources. A new image made with the Low Frequency Array, or LOFAR, resolves an extraordinary amount of that hidden activity. By combining new high-resolution observations with an earlier deep radio map, astronomers assembled a catalogue of **62,916 distinct radio sources** in a field called ELAIS-N1.

The region covers about 6.25 square degrees, or roughly 25 times the apparent area of the full Moon. It contains galaxies whose central black holes launch enormous jets, alongside galaxies where stars are forming. The catalogue is not a claim that every object was previously unknown. Its advance is the unusually detailed, sensitive view of a well-studied region.

## How an array of antennas makes a picture

Radio telescopes detect wavelengths much longer than visible light. LOFAR combines signals from many antennas spread across Europe, effectively using their separation to sharpen its view. The team analyzed 200 hours of observations at frequencies between 115 and 168 megahertz.

Their sharpest images distinguish structures separated by less than half an arcsecond, a tiny fraction of a degree. The central image reaches a point-source sensitivity of 5.3 microjanskys per beam at a resolution of 0.33 by 0.39 arcseconds. A jansky measures the strength of radio emission arriving at a telescope; a microjansky is one millionth of that unit. Such faint signals demand careful calibration.

Radio waves arriving at widely separated antennas do not automatically fit together into a clean picture. The Earth's ionosphere can distort their apparent directions, while instrumental effects change the recorded signal. The researchers used advances in long-baseline calibration and image processing, then checked their positions against 95 quasars in the Gaia reference frame. The result is a map with both fine detail and accurate source positions.

## Why the extra detail matters

A fuzzy patch in an older radio image might represent a galaxy's star-forming disk, a jet emerging from its central black hole, or several neighboring sources blended together. Sharper imaging helps distinguish those possibilities. This matters because black-hole jets can push energy into surrounding gas, while radio emission from star formation can reveal activity hidden behind dust.

The new data also create opportunities for comparisons with optical, infrared and X-ray observations of the same field. Astronomers can connect radio structures with host galaxies, estimate their distances where supporting measurements exist, and investigate how galaxies change over time.

The study also tests whether such demanding images can be produced at practical computational cost. Its authors report that a wide, ultra-deep radio image at sub-arcsecond resolution is now feasible, helping prepare the way for upgraded LOFAR observations and future Square Kilometre Array surveys.

## What remains uncertain

This is a technical and observational milestone rather than proof of a new theory about galaxy evolution. A radio source is not necessarily a separate galaxy, and the map alone does not establish the distance or physical origin of every detection. Follow-up measurements and comparisons across wavelengths will turn this detailed inventory into answers about star formation and black-hole activity.

The paper first appeared on arXiv on November 4, 2026 and was reported as accepted by *Astronomy & Astrophysics*. Its preprint results should be read with that publication status in mind.
